Holzbaurechner / Deck stairs

Deck stair calculator

Measure the height from the deck surface to the ground and get the number of steps, the riser height, the run, the stringer length and the lumber you need, checked against the code limits.

The code limits for deck stairs

The International Residential Code sets the basic dimensions for stairs at a house, and they apply to deck stairs as well:

  • Riser height: no more than 7-3/4 in. The tallest and the shortest riser in a flight may differ by no more than 3/8 in.
  • Tread depth: at least 10 in., measured from nosing to nosing.
  • Nosing: 3/4 to 1-1/4 in. on stairs with closed risers.
  • Width: at least 36 in.
  • Handrail: required on stairs with four or more risers, 34 to 38 in. above the nosings.

The calculator spreads the total rise evenly over the risers, starting from your target height, and checks that no riser exceeds 7-3/4 in.

How the stairs are built

The stairs hang on the deck rim joist with stringers cut from 2x12s. Each tread is made of two 2x6 or two composite boards, which gives a tread of about 11-1/4 in. with a 1 in. nosing over the riser below. The deck surface counts as the top step, so a flight with four risers has three treads.

The AWC deck guide DCA 6 limits cut 2x12 stringers to a horizontal span of 6 ft and a spacing of 18 in. Composite treads usually need stringers every 12 in. If the stairs run farther than 6 ft, support the stringers in the middle with a beam on posts or add a landing. After cutting, at least 5 in. of solid wood (the throat) should remain below the notches.

Laying out a stringer

Use a framing square with stair gauges set to the riser height on the tongue and the run on the blade. Mark each step, then take the thickness of one tread off the bottom of the stringer so the first step is not taller than the others. Cut the first stringer, check it in place and use it as the template for the rest.

Building the stairs step by step

  1. Measure the rise: from the top of the decking straight down to where the bottom step will land. On a slope, measure at the landing spot, not at the deck.
  2. Prepare the landing: a concrete pad or compacted gravel with pavers, so the stringers never sit on soil.
  3. Cut the stringers: lay out and cut one, test it, then copy it.
  4. Attach the stringers: hang them on the rim joist with stair stringer connectors and fasten the bottom to the landing.
  5. Treads and risers: screw the treads on with two screws per stringer and board, then add riser boards if you want closed risers.
  6. Handrail and guards: add posts, a graspable handrail and balusters before anyone uses the stairs.

Frequently asked questions

How many steps do I need for a 30 in. high deck?
Four risers of 7-1/2 in. and three treads. With a run of about 10-1/4 in. per tread the stairs reach about 2 ft 7 in. out from the deck.
How long a 2x12 do I need for deck stair stringers?
Add up the total rise and the total run, take the diagonal and add about a foot for the cuts at top and bottom. For a 30 in. rise that is about 4 ft 7 in., so a 10 ft 2x12 gives two stringers.
How far apart should stair stringers be?
No more than 18 in. for wood treads according to DCA 6, which means three stringers for a 36 in. wide stair. Composite treads usually need 12 in., so four stringers for the same width.
Do deck stairs need a handrail?
Yes, as soon as there are four or more risers. Stairs more than 30 in. above the ground also need guards on the open sides.

Lumber sizes follow the span tables of the 2021 International Residential Code (IRC) and are planning values. They do not replace a permit review or an engineer. Decks, patio covers and carports usually need a building permit, so check with your local building department.
